st.t: AI procurement: Deployed outcomes outrank adoption counts
st.an: The source accepts that deployed outcomes should outrank adoption counts and vendor demonstrations, then materially develops the proposition through a public-law framework for causal testing, risk-tiered lifecycle evaluation, ongoing quality assurance, independent review and enforceable contractual access to evaluation materials.
qs: Third, causal methods address the fundamental epistemic uncertainty about how AI systems will affect outcomes in the real world, moving beyond predictions about what might happen to evidence about what does happen once these systems are deployed.

Buyers should refuse “no testing” provisions, insist on clauses that expressly permit experimentation and external evaluation, and treat access to evaluation artifacts—test suites, error analyses, quality-assurance plans—as part of the product rather than a discretionary add-on.

st.t: Federal procurement: Acquisition speed can weaken accountability
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s emphasis on continuing, use-case-specific evaluation and enforceable vendor accountability, then materially develops it by grounding those duties in administrative and procurement law. It also proposes stronger contractual rules against restrictions on testing and independent scrutiny, while identifying agency capacity and resourcing as implementation constraints.
qs: By situating AI evaluation within the wider landscape of federal performance measurement, evidence-based policymaking, and procurement quality assurance, we argue that effective AI governance requires reconnecting the emerging AI toolkit with longstanding evaluation obligations in administrative and procurement law.

Congress and OMB could make explicit that “no testing” or “no benchmarking” clauses in rights- and safety-impacting AI contracts are contrary to public policy and unenforceable, much as certain indemnification and nondisclosure terms already are.

st.t: Judgment development: AI exposure is not professional readiness
st.an: The source reinforces the distinction between adopting AI and being institutionally prepared to govern it, adding a concrete procurement constraint: licensing terms can prevent evaluation even where substantial expertise exists. This materially extends the cluster’s implementation argument that responsible AI education requires freedom to scrutinize tools, not merely access to them.
qs: But buried in the licensing terms was a startling clause: The school—an elite institution with faculty experts in AI governance, a standing AI committee, and a mission to interrogate emerging technologies—was prohibited from conducting any “test or review” of the system.
1 ^Lthe eagerness to be early adopters, the institution had nearly contracted away the most basic element of responsible governance: the ability to understand how the system behaved.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s caution against inferring real-world benefits from adoption, benchmarks or short tests, and materially extends its deployment recommendations by grounding continuous, risk-tailored evaluation in public-law authority, institutional independence and adequate resourcing.
qs: This Article argues that effective AI governance must be built around legally grounded, ongoing evaluation rather than episodic or purely technical assessment.
For evaluation to produce meaningful oversight, central institutional challenges of independence and resourcing must be overcome, coupled with necessary technical advances.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s use-context-specific, lifecycle governance proposition and materially develops it with a legally grounded, three-tiered evaluation framework covering performance measurement, ongoing quality assurance, and rigorous testing for high-stakes deployments. It also specifies independence, resourcing, procurement rights, and post-deployment monitoring as institutional requirements.
qs: This Article argues that effective AI governance must be built around legally grounded, ongoing evaluation rather than episodic or purely technical assessment.
Taken together, these methods offer a three-tiered risk-based evaluation framework with relevant levels of evaluation rigor.

st.t: Agent benchmarks: Protocol scores are not competence
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal claim that benchmark scores do not by themselves establish real-world competence or deployment readiness. It emphasizes context and task mismatch, static-test limitations, leakage, drift and saturation, while warning that broader safety and impact metrics still leave core validity problems unresolved.
qs: First, because benchmarks evaluate for static outputs, they are unable to capture real usage conditions, including user interactions, adversarial inputs, or model and data drift, all of which are increasingly important for evaluation of multimodal AI applications in the wild.
Benchmarks now exist that take a more holistic view of a system’s performance, but even such welcome improvements still suffer from the other limitations discussed.

st.t: Evaluation validity: Benchmark safeguards impose trade-offs
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s central proposition: benchmarks enable standardised, reproducible comparisons but cannot by themselves establish real-world performance, professional competence or deployment safety. It specifically identifies contextual mismatch, data leakage, saturation and narrow technical metrics, while welcoming broader safety and impact measures without treating them as a complete remedy.
qs: Benchmarks have gained popularity as they provide standardized, scalable, and reproducible metrics across models, teams, and time.10

kp.k: AI adoption outpaces rigorous evaluation, including in legal institutions
kp.d: The authors argue that sophisticated institutions often adopt AI without establishing its practical value. Their opening anecdote concerns an unnamed law school nearly accepting a license prohibiting evaluation; a footnote states that last-minute negotiations removed the restriction. Separately, they cite May 2024 reporting on Paul Weiss suggesting that more than a year of piloting a bespoke legal assistant had not generated rigorous metrics connecting use to productivity or bottom-line performance. These examples illustrate evaluation deficiencies rather than demonstrated absence of benefits.
qs: AI adoption is accelerating far faster than evaluation practices, even in our most sophisticated institutions.
After last-minute negotiations, the usage restrictions were removed.

But public reporting suggests that this experimentation has proceeded without rigorous metrics tying the tool to concrete productivity gains or bottom-line performance, underscoring how even sophisticated private actors treat evaluation as optional, informal, and largely inward-facing.

kp.k: Adoption figures do not establish realized benefits
kp.d: The paper reports that a 2024 McKinsey survey found AI use in at least one business function at 78% of surveyed companies, versus 55% in 2023. Federal agencies reported 1,700 AI use cases in 2024, more than double 2023, with more than 10% labeled rights- or safety-impacting. A 2025 ICF survey found 41% running small-scale pilots, 16% actively scaling efforts and only 8% seeing results from mature programs. The authors suggest that client pressure for lower costs and shorter timelines will sustain adoption, but do not treat these figures as causal evidence of savings.
qs: A 2024 McKinsey survey found that 78% of companies surveyed reported using AI in at least one business function, up from 55% in 2023.
A 2025 ICF survey of federal agencies found that 41% are running small-scale AI pilots, 16% are actively scaling AI efforts, but only 8% are seeing results from mature programs.

kp.k: Benchmarks poorly capture contextual performance and downstream impact
kp.d: The authors recognize benchmarks' standardization, scalability and reproducibility, but identify static outputs, inadequate task-specific data, decontextualized proxies such as bar-test performance for legal reasoning, data leakage and performance saturation as limitations. They argue that technical accuracy, robustness and latency do not establish benefits, distributional effects or institutional outcomes, even when supplemented by broader trust and safety benchmarks.
qs: First, because benchmarks evaluate for static outputs, they are unable to capture real usage conditions, including user interactions, adversarial inputs, or model and data drift, all of which are increasingly important for evaluation of multimodal AI applications in the wild.
Third, data leakage, wherein a model is trained on test data, can result in overly-optimistic benchmarking results, but poor performance in real-world deployments.

kp.k: System-level causal evaluation must supplement conventional AI assessments
kp.d: The paper characterizes benchmarking, red teaming, impact assessments and audits as typically descriptive or observational rather than causal. It argues that component accuracy cannot establish whether deployment improves outcomes, because workflow integration and human responses matter. Its clinical example distinguishes diagnostic accuracy from effects on misdiagnosis, patient health, length of stay and cost-effectiveness. The authors recommend comparisons against existing human practices, including their biases and errors, rather than unrealistic standards of perfection.
qs: For example, benchmarking helps us understand whether an AI model is achieving accuracy scores on diagnostic tasks, but not whether deploying that model causally reduces (or increases) misdiagnosis rates in clinical practice.
First, such methods allow for performance-oriented assessments of AI integrations, measuring an AI system’s outcomes against human baselines rather than abstract standards.

Third, causal methods address the fundamental epistemic uncertainty about how AI systems will affect outcomes in the real world, moving beyond predictions about what might happen to evidence about what does happen once these systems are deployed.

kp.k: Federal AI requirements advance oversight but remain politically vulnerable
kp.d: The authors describe continuity between Biden-era OMB requirements and the 2025 framework: realistic pre-deployment testing, impact assessments, internal independent review and ongoing monitoring. They report that M-25-21 replaced rights- and safety-impacting categories with high-impact AI, while procurement guidance added performance-focused quality assurance. These are described as important advances over private-sector norms, but vulnerable because they rest on executive action rather than statute. The paper identifies uncertainty following the AI Safety Institute's June 2025 rebranding as CAISI and reports a DHS Inspector General finding that DHS lacked an implementation plan for its AI strategy.
qs: Under the second Trump Administration, OMB memo M-25-21 explicitly rescinded “rights- impacting” and “safety-impacting” categories
because these obligations rest on executive orders and OMB guidance rather than statute, they can be reinterpreted or rescinded with each administration.

kp.k: Multi-method testing reveals differences that individual methods miss
kp.d: The paper cites NIST's November 2025 ARIA pilot as evidence for combining model testing, red teaming and field testing. It evaluated seven applications from five organizations across three proxy scenarios, involved 51 red teamers and 19 field testers, and generated over 1,500 expert annotations. Divergent expert and user assessments support the authors' argument for multiple evaluation methods. They qualify the institutional lesson by noting that there was not yet public evidence that ARIA's proposed subsequent iterations were being pursued after reorganization.
qs: Testing involved 51 red teamers and 19 field testers and generated over 1,500 expert annotations.

For one application, field testers perceived greater validity risk (5.00/10) than annotators observed (3.58/10); for another application, the pattern reversed, with annotators recording higher risk (3.52/10) than red teamers perceived (2.24/10).

kp.k: Existing public law supplies an evaluation framework
kp.d: The central legal argument is that AI governance should reconnect technical assessment with existing federal performance measurement, evidence-building and procurement obligations. The authors identify GPRA, the Evidence Act and procurement and IT investment law as sources of authority and institutional design principles. They present these frameworks as relevant beyond government, while emphasizing that legal authority has not translated consistently into substantive evaluation.
qs: Federal law already contains multiple frameworks that, at least on paper, require agencies to evaluate their programs, policies, and technology acquisitions.
Throughout the Article, we draw heavily on public law frameworks. However, our aim is to inform AI evaluation and governance across sectors—public and private.

kp.k: Performance measurement can expose outcomes or encourage metric gaming
kp.d: GPRA offers multidimensional indicators, reliable data, transparency, comparisons with goals and analysis of failures. The authors nevertheless describe implementation as frequently procedural, with incentives to choose easily achieved targets. They illustrate missing trade-offs through SSA's performance plan: its target of 215 days for initial disability claims and emphasis on automation are not matched by measures of automated decision accuracy, error patterns or distributional effects. The proposed remedy is to connect meaningful performance measures to vendor milestones rather than treat reporting as compliance.
qs: Most importantly, GPRA’s attempt to link performance metrics and budgets created perverse incentives.
Yet the performance plan is largely silent on how the quality or accuracy of these automated interventions will be measured.
Agencies could achieve this by linking GPRA-style performance measures to performance-based contracts, with set milestones for vendors to meet at stages within a contract.

kp.k: Benefits administration trial challenges satisfaction-based adoption decisions
kp.d: The authors discuss a randomized demonstration project involving Stanford RegLab, the Colorado Department of Labor and Employment and the U.S. Department of Labor. They report improvements over historical baselines and favorable reviewer feedback, but no improvement in the hypothesized time-efficiency outcome in the controlled comparison. The trial also suggests, rather than establishes conclusively here, reduced inter-reviewer variability. The lesson is that user acceptance and historical comparisons cannot substitute for rigorous evaluation of AI-assisted benefits adjudication.
qs: The trial further suggests that the system may reduce inter- reviewer variability, a metric that is arguably deeply important given staffing constraints and surging benefits caseloads.

Organizations typically rely on non-randomized user acceptance test results before rolling out a tool; however, the findings of the CDLE trial show that user satisfaction metrics are necessary but insufficient indicators that a tool or system should be purchased or deployed.

kp.k: Evidence Act implementation largely overlooks deployed AI systems
kp.d: The Evidence Act requires learning agendas, evaluation plans and designated officials, and provides a framework for rigorous pilots and impact studies. The authors find that agency plans largely omit AI despite expanding deployment: DHS reported 26 rights-impacting applications in 2024, but its 2025 evaluation plan mentioned neither those systems nor AI. They also report that Labor's plan fell from 26 projects in 2023–2024 to two in fiscal 2026. Resource constraints are central: Treasury reportedly had fewer than five dedicated full-time evaluation personnel despite over 100,000 staff. The authors attribute weak implementation to funding, capacity, independence and broad agency discretion.
qs: Most strikingly for AI, agencies’ evaluation plans are largely silent about AI systems, even as AI deployments proliferate.

Treasury exemplifies the resource problem: despite employing over 100,000 staff, the department has fewer than five dedicated full-time evaluation personnel after funding requests for a central evidence coordination team were rejected.

kp.k: Procurement can require vendor evidence and continuous quality assurance
kp.d: The authors interpret FAR provisions as supporting prototypes, pilots, defined performance standards, quality-assurance surveillance plans, modular contracting and contractor evidence of conformity. They argue that these mechanisms can shift evidentiary responsibility toward vendors. However, operational metrics may still miss substantive harms: the cited CBP Automated Targeting System business case tracked measures such as uptime and narcotics seizures but omitted accuracy and false positives. Procurement therefore offers a legal foundation, not proof that meaningful evaluation already occurs.
qs: Thus, FAR puts the burden of proof on AI vendors, instead of the purchasing agency – an important distinction given agencies’ resourcing constraints.
Yet nowhere in these performance measures is any metric of the accuracy of the system or false positives, nor is there any measure relating to timeliness.

In short, procurement and IT investment law are a natural legal home for AI testing and evaluation, but current practice often treats their evaluation hooks as flexible, easily satisfied paperwork requirements.

kp.k: Evaluation rigor should scale with deployment risk
kp.d: The proposed three-tier framework combines performance measurement for all AI projects, more active procurement-backed quality assurance, and rigorous pilots or randomized trials for high-stakes, high-priority deployments. The authors recommend mixing methods, including random holdout sets within quality assurance, to investigate causal effects while monitoring drift and degradation. They also propose independent access to vendor testing data and consideration of third-party evaluators; the cited experimental evidence for more truthful independent audits comes from pollution auditing in India, not an AI deployment trial.
qs: Taken together, these methods offer a three-tiered risk-based evaluation framework with relevant levels of evaluation rigor.
Finally, for high-stakes, high-priority projects, federal agencies can conduct impact evaluation using rigorous pilot testing or RCTs, similar to the CDLE demonstration project.
For example, QA can be matched with other evaluation mechanisms to establish causality, for example, incorporating random hold out sets to test the impact of a new AI feature,

kp.k: Independent evaluation requires institutions, funding and technical capacity
kp.d: The paper identifies independence from builders and operators and resources commensurate with risk as the main institutional challenges. Recommendations include context-specific research methods, an independent nonprofit modeled on MDRC, a philanthropic spend-down AI Evaluation Fund and temporary academic or technical appointments through the Intergovernmental Personnel Act. GSA's Office of Evaluation Sciences is offered as a historical capacity-building model, having completed over 120 cross-agency evaluations since 2015; the paper's footnote qualifies this example by stating that OES no longer exists under the second Trump administration.
qs: two design challenges dominate: ensuring that evaluation is independent of the actors who build and operate AI systems and resourcing that evaluation at a scale commensurate with the stakes.

A dedicated “AI Evaluation Fund,” structured as a spend-down vehicle, could seed these efforts, support durable collaborations between agencies and external researchers, and absorb the upfront costs of rapid, iterative evaluation cycles that conventional program evaluation timelines cannot accommodate.
Unfortunately, under the second Trump Administration, OES no longer exists.

kp.k: Testing rights should become standard AI contract terms
kp.d: For private purchasers, including legal institutions, the authors recommend refusing restrictions on testing and securing express rights to experimentation, external evaluation and access to evaluation materials. For government, they propose making no-testing and no-benchmarking clauses unenforceable in rights- and safety-impacting contracts and clarifying that protected disclosure may include agency-retained independent evaluators. These are recommendations extending beyond the paper's account of existing procurement requirements, not assertions that every such restriction is already invalid.
qs: Buyers should refuse “no testing” provisions, insist on clauses that expressly permit experimentation and external evaluation, and treat access to evaluation artifacts—test suites, error analyses, quality-assurance plans—as part of the product rather than a discretionary add-on.

Congress and OMB could make explicit that “no testing” or “no benchmarking” clauses in rights- and safety-impacting AI contracts are contrary to public policy and unenforceable, much as certain indemnification and nondisclosure terms already are.

kp.k: Credible outcome evidence could reshape vendor competition
kp.d: The authors contrast technology firms' routine experiments on minor product changes with AI deployment based on demonstrations, benchmarks and anecdotes. They recommend testing AI-enabled workflows against business or service objectives and independent review for consequential decisions. Their prediction is conditional: evaluation could shift competition from marketing toward demonstrated performance, reduce uncertainty and accelerate diffusion of useful tools, while acknowledging that procedural requirements can slow innovation.
qs: Private deployers can close this gap by treating model deployment the way they already treat user-facing features: as a decision that should rest on structured testing against clear outcome metrics.
Vendors, in turn, can differentiate themselves by embracing independent verification and validation for their systems and by publishing credible evidence of model performance in realistic settings.
Yet evaluation can also be innovation-forcing: it shifts competition away from marketing claims and toward demonstrated performance in the contexts where systems will be used.

kp.k: Agentic autonomy strengthens the need for lifecycle monitoring
kp.d: The authors acknowledge that autonomous, dynamic systems complicate evaluation because performance depends on end-to-end workflows, changing environments and interactions with users and downstream systems. They argue that this reinforces rather than defeats their framework: realistic pilots, procurement-backed surveillance, access to logs and artifacts, and downstream outcome measures should test whether workflows remain within specified tolerances for accuracy, safety, escalation and recovery.
qs: Agentic systems do make evaluation harder, because performance depends on end-to-end workflows, shifting environments, and interactions with users and downstream systems.
But that is precisely why this Article centers lifecycle, system-level evaluation rather than one-shot model assessment.
As autonomy increases, continuous monitoring becomes a basic condition of control.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Ho, Martin and Tagal argue that AI adoption is outpacing credible evaluation, including in legal institutions, and that its actual value must be established through ongoing, context-specific evaluation rather than inferred from benchmarks or demonstrations.
pts.d: The authors describe a law school nearly accepting a license prohibiting testing and a leading law firm's extended pilot without publicly reported rigorous productivity or bottom-line metrics. These examples support a claim about inadequate evaluation, not a finding that legal AI cannot improve productivity. Across public and private deployments, they argue that static benchmarks cannot establish downstream benefits or causal effects. Their benefits-administration example illustrates the difference: favorable reviewer feedback and improvements relative to historical baselines did not establish the hypothesized time-efficiency improvement in the randomized trial, although the system may reduce inter-reviewer variability. They propose using existing public-law frameworks to support risk-tailored performance measurement, quality assurance and rigorous impact evaluation. They further predict, conditionally, that credible evaluation could shift competition toward demonstrated performance, lower iteration costs and accelerate adoption of genuinely useful tools. For agentic systems, they claim increasing autonomy makes continuous, workflow-level monitoring more important.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The authors combine institutional examples, reported adoption statistics, cited experimental findings, technical literature and legal analysis; their proposed market effects are predictions rather than measured findings.
pts.d: The law-school licensing episode is an unnamed institutional vignette; the authors report that negotiations removed the restriction. The law-firm example draws on May 2024 Bloomberg Law reporting about Paul Weiss, rather than an independently measured productivity result. For adoption, they cite a McKinsey survey reporting 78% of surveyed companies using AI in at least one business function in 2024, versus 55% in 2023, and federal reporting of 1,700 AI use cases in 2024. Their principal causal-evaluation illustration is the Stanford RegLab–Colorado Department of Labor and Employment–U.S. Department of Labor demonstration project, cited as forthcoming in 2026. They also use NIST's ARIA pilot to illustrate differences between expert annotations and user perceptions. The governance argument draws on GPRA, the Evidence Act, procurement and IT investment law, executive guidance, GAO reports and agency evaluation plans. For example, they contrast DHS's 26 reported rights-impacting AI applications in 2024 with their absence from its 2025 evaluation plan. The paper supplies no measured legal-market growth, lawyer displacement or firm-profitability effect, and no experimental estimate for the predicted competitive benefits of evaluation.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The diagnosis concerns deployments and governance developments principally documented during 2023–2025; proposed improvements are prospective, conditional and not assigned a fixed realization date.
pts.d: The 2026 working paper discusses adoption surveys, executive guidance, institutional changes and evaluation plans extending into fiscal 2026. It reports that the law-firm pilot had lasted more than a year in the cited 2024 reporting. Its proposed evaluation regime spans pre-deployment testing, controlled or early deployment trials, and ongoing post-deployment monitoring. The authors reserve resource-intensive impact evaluation for high-stakes, high-priority projects and favor lower-investment performance measurement more broadly. They expressly acknowledge that evaluation can slow innovation through proceduralism, that statutory evaluation frameworks can become compliance exercises, and that executive-based obligations are vulnerable to administrative change. Their predicted benefits depend on evaluator independence, sustained resources, usable data infrastructure, outcome-specific metrics, enforceable testing rights and consequences for inadequate performance. Agentic AI strengthens the case for lifecycle monitoring because behavior depends on changing environments and end-to-end interactions.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims concern legal institutions as AI buyers, public agencies and their service users, private deployers and vendors, and the researchers and funders needed to build evaluation capacity.
pts.d: Law schools risk losing the ability to study purchased tools, while law firms face pressure to adopt AI as a perceived means of reducing costs and timelines without necessarily establishing those savings. Federal agencies must assess whether AI improves actual program outcomes, including the accuracy and distributional effects of benefits adjudication, screening and other consequential decisions. Benefits reviewers and claimants are affected by possible changes in processing efficiency and consistency; the paper does not establish that such gains always occur. Public and private buyers would need to secure testing rights and evaluate workflows against service or business objectives. Vendors would face demands for performance evidence, access to evaluation artifacts and ongoing quality surveillance, while potentially differentiating themselves through credible independent evaluation. Researchers, philanthropic funders and independent evaluation institutions would supply methods, financing and capacity. The paper does not predict changes to law-firm staffing structures, billing models or lawyer employment.
